title: Powers and roots
summary: To square a number, multiply it by itself; to cube it, use it three times in a product. A [[square-root|square root]] undoes squaring and a [[cube-root|cube root]] undoes cubing. Learn the common ones by heart for the non-calculator papers.

goals.text: Square a number, and find square roots, including the negative root.
Cube a number, and find cube roots, including roots of negative numbers.
Recall the squares up to $15^{2}$ and the cubes of $1$ to $5$ and $10$.
Work out other powers and roots, by hand and on a calculator.

before.prompt: Which of these is a [[square-number|square number]]?
before.hint: Which one is a whole number times itself?
before.explain: $36 = 6 \times 6$. The others are not a whole number times itself. Revise it in {{lesson:1.1}}.

before.prompt: Which of these is a [[cube-number|cube number]]?

blocks.text: To square a number, multiply it by itself. $7^{2}$, said "7 squared", means $7 \times 7 = 49$.
Squaring a [[natural-number|natural number]] gives a [[square-number|square number]]. It is the area of a square with that side length.

blocks.alt: Left: a square made of 5 rows of 5 small squares, 25 in all, with each side labelled 5. Below it: area 25, so the side is the square root of 25, which is 5. Right: a cube with each edge labelled 3. Below it: volume 27, so the edge is the cube root of 27, which is 3.
blocks.caption: A root takes you from the area or volume back to the side.

blocks.statement: A [[square-root|square root]] of $n$ is a number that gives $n$ when you square it. The sign $\sqrt{n}$ means the positive square root, and $\sqrt{0} = 0$.
blocks.plain: The side of a square with area $n$.

blocks.text: Every positive number has two square roots. $6^{2} = 36$ and $(-6)^{2} = 36$, so the square roots of $36$ are $6$ and $-6$, written $\pm 6$. But $\sqrt{36}$ is $6$ only.
With no calculator, you need the squares from $1^{2}$ to $15^{2}$ by heart. Then you can read square roots straight back: $\sqrt{196} = 14$.
For a decimal, ignore the point first. If the digits make a square number and there is an even number of decimal places, the root has half as many decimal places.

blocks.question: Without a calculator, find $\sqrt{2.25}$.
steps: $2.25$ has 2 decimal places, so the root has 1: $1.5$.

blocks.text: Halving is not square rooting: $\sqrt{64}$ is $8$, not $32$. Square your answer to check it.

blocks.hint: Which number squared gives $9$? Then count decimal places.
blocks.explain: $3^{2} = 9$, and $0.09$ has 2 decimal places, so the root has 1. Check: $0.3 \times 0.3 = 0.09$.

blocks.hint: $144$ has two square roots. Which one is negative?

blocks.text: To cube a number, use it three times in a product. $4^{3}$, said "4 cubed", means $4 \times 4 \times 4 = 64$.
Cubing a natural number gives a [[cube-number|cube number]]. It is the volume of a cube with that edge length.

blocks.statement: The [[cube-root|cube root]] of $n$, written $\sqrt[3]{n}$, is the number that gives $n$ when you cube it.
blocks.plain: The edge of a cube with volume $n$.

blocks.text: Every number has exactly one cube root. A negative number has a negative cube root: $(-3)^{3} = -27$, so $\sqrt[3]{-27} = -3$.
Learn these six cubes. They let you write down cube roots such as $\sqrt[3]{125} = 5$ with no calculator.
$2^{3}$ is not $2 \times 3 = 6$. The small $3$ says how many $2$s to multiply: $2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$.
Decimals work as for square roots. If the digits make a cube number and the number of decimal places is a multiple of 3, the root has a third as many.

blocks.question: Without a calculator, find $\sqrt[3]{0.008}$.
steps: $0.008$ has 3 decimal places, so the root has 1: $0.2$.

blocks.hint: Which number, used three times in a product, gives $-1000$?
blocks.explain: $(-10) \times (-10) \times (-10) = 100 \times (-10) = -1000$. A negative number has a negative cube root.

blocks.text: In $3^{5}$, $3$ is the base and $5$ is the power, or [[index|index]]. It means five $3$s multiplied: $3 \times 3 \times 3 \times 3 \times 3 = 243$.
Roots undo powers. $\sqrt[4]{16}$ is the fourth root of $16$. It is $2$, because $2^{4} = 16$.

An even root ($\sqrt{\;}$, $\sqrt[4]{\;}$, …) of a positive number means the positive one. An odd root ($\sqrt[3]{\;}$, $\sqrt[5]{\;}$, …) works for negative numbers too. A negative number has no even root.
Do powers after brackets, but before $\times$, $\div$, $+$ and $-$. So $2 \times 3^{2} = 2 \times 9 = 18$, but $(2 \times 3)^{2} = 6^{2} = 36$.

blocks.question: Work out $2^{6} - 6^{2}$.
steps: Start at $1$ and double six times: $2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64$. So $2^{6} = 64$.

blocks.hint: Find a number whose fourth power is $10\,000$.

blocks.text: On Papers 3 and 4, use the calculator's power and root keys. Keep every digit until the end, then round to 3 significant figures.

blocks.question: Use your calculator to work out $\sqrt[5]{300} + 1.6^{3}$. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
steps: Round to 3 significant figures: $7.23$. Sense check: $3^{5} = 243$, so the root is a little over $3$.

blocks.prompt: Use your calculator to work out $2.3^{4} - \sqrt[3]{50}$. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
blocks.hint: Find each part, keep all the digits, then subtract.

blocks.text: Extended students also write roots as powers, such as $\sqrt[4]{16} = 16^{\frac{1}{4}}$.
$\sqrt{n}$ is the positive square root. A positive number $n$ has two square roots, $\pm\sqrt{n}$: $\pm 7$ for $49$.
A negative number has one cube root, and it is negative: $\sqrt[3]{-8} = -2$.
$a^{n}$ means $n$ copies of $a$ multiplied: $2^{3} = 2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$, not $2 \times 3$.
Powers come after brackets, but before $\times$, $\div$, $+$ and $-$.
Check a root by raising it to the power: $1.5^{2} = 2.25$, so $\sqrt{2.25} = 1.5$.

mistakes: Multiplying the base by the power: $10^{3} = 30$. Write out the product: $10 \times 10 \times 10 = 1000$.
Halving instead of rooting: $\sqrt{64} = 32$. Ask which number times itself gives $64$: it is $8$.
Giving $n = \pm 11$ when the question says $n$ is positive. Read the condition: $n^{2} = 121$ with $n > 0$ gives $n = 11$ only.
Misplacing the decimal point: $\sqrt{0.36} = 0.06$. Square your answer to check: $0.6^{2} = 0.36$.
Dividing by $3$ instead of taking a cube root: $\sqrt[3]{27}$ is $3$, not $27 \div 3 = 9$.
Adding first inside a bracket such as $(5 + 2 \times 4)^{2}$. Multiply first: $5 + 8 = 13$, so the answer is $13^{2} = 169$.
examTips: Write down the value: no working is needed. Know the squares to $15^{2}$ and the cubes of $1$ to $5$ and $10$, so the mark is quick.
Work out, with no calculator: write each root and power as a number first, then combine them. Check each root by squaring or cubing back.
Give your answer to 3 significant figures: keep the full calculator value until the end. Rounding $\sqrt[5]{300}$ to $3.1$ first gives $7.20$, not $7.23$.
